articles.title: Selling The Skinny
articles.content:
连续三年，我在这些版面上探讨过与我们时代定义性药物——GLP-1类药物相关的专利问题。现在，让我们进入第四年。2023年，我关注了体重减轻领域的两大巨头——诺和诺德和礼来（Eli Lilly）最近获得的专利，它们正在不断扩充其保护Ozempic/Wegovy和Mounjaro/Zepbound畅销药品的专利组合。次年，我分析了试图争夺GLP-1药物巨大需求的仿制药公司的失败努力。（此后，仿制版Ozempic已可获得，但需要乘坐加拿大航空或印度航空才能获取。）去年，我报道了礼来对一家大型复方药房提起的诉讼，这是GLP-1制造商针对复方药房的多线（法院和FDA）战争的重大升级，复方药房以较低价格提供的药品抽走了约10%的处方量。

如今，随着来自复方药房和仿制药的威胁基本得到控制，我们可以关注GLP-1领域最新消息——一家大品牌对另一家提出的令人惊讶的虚假广告投诉。在此之前，值得一提的是，自从我的2023年专栏发表以来，礼来的股价几乎翻了三倍，达到当前水平，而诺和诺德的股价则出现了显著下跌。即便如此，诺和诺德的GLP-1收入自那以来也翻了一番，这说明这两种药物对两家公司的重要性依然存在。

尽管诺和诺德的Ozempic/Wegovy品牌取得了成功，但礼来在股价涨幅方面的优势与其Mounjaro/Zepbound产品的收入增长相呼应。预计后者的收入将在2026年达到约450亿美元，较2023年增长近九倍。虽然礼来在市场份额方面占据了更大份额，但诺和诺德认为，礼来的部分成功得益于虚假广告，误导消费者相信礼来产品的相对疗效远高于诺和诺德的产品。根据诺和诺德的说法，在适当比较下，竞争产品之间的体重减轻潜力差异并不大。在诺和诺德看来，如果告诉真相，大多数患者会选择副作用较少或定价更好的药物，而不是坚持选择礼来的产品，仅仅因为误以为它们会导致更多的体重减轻。考虑到GLP-1患者通常需要长期坚持使用选择的药物，纠正误解对诺和诺德来说非常重要，因为它试图在下一代GLP-1药物推出之前争取尽可能多的市场份额。为此，诺和诺德上周在新泽西州地区法院提起了虚假广告诉讼，并不久后提出了预审禁令动议。

媒体对诺和诺德提起诉讼的反应迅速，这正是诺和诺德所预期并几乎肯定欢迎的。本人甚至被邀请与一家领先的丹麦商业出版物分享对诺和诺德提起诉讼的看法。诺和诺德的提起诉讼可以被视为一种有效的反广告形式，诺和诺德传递的信息是，礼来不得不依赖虚假声明来制造与Ozempic/Wegovy的竞争优势。对于消费者来说，认为礼来的广告“虚假到被起诉”的想法是一个容易理解的信息，有助于通过围绕提起诉讼的媒体关注，为诺和诺德创造有效的广告。再加上诺和诺德在提起诉讼前向礼来发出了停止令，要求礼来对其广告进行某些更改，这使得消费者理解诺和诺德只是在礼来的固执下，将法律行动作为最后手段。与此同时，礼来至少部分同意对其广告进行一些更改，这可能为礼来后来的论点奠定了基础，即诺和诺德的主张过于夸张，礼来在争端中是商业和法律上负责的一方。

然而，任何法律行动的原告都需要在媒体关注之后取得一些实质性进展，特别是在预审禁令的情况下。在这里，诺和诺德认为礼来依赖过时的临床研究结果和刻意剂量误导比较，制造其产品优越的叙事。对于诺和诺德来说，损害被放大了，因为礼来营销的规模和覆盖面，无论是社交媒体还是电视广告。因此，诺和诺德的法律团队Debevoise和Plimpton要求法院禁止礼来运行其当前广告。它甚至走得更远，建议法院命令礼来进行纠正性广告。礼来方面则承诺在案件推进中进行激烈反击。

最终，我认为这次提起诉讼反映了诺和诺德对GLP-1市场在美国发展阶段的认识，即这两家巨头正在争夺每张处方。随着来自复方GLP-1和仿制药的威胁已被降低到可管理的水平，诺和诺德的投诉和预审禁令要求表明，诺和诺德必须在争夺和维持市场份额方面对礼来采取更积极的行动——在下一代更先进的GLP-1药物推出之前，每一个患者的签约都是至关重要的。幸运的是，无论法律结果如何，患者在减肥和糖尿病管理方面都有选择的余地。市场顶端的双寡头格局不会因这一案件而受到威胁。然而，争议的焦点在于这些公司如何在争夺更多市场份额的过程中投放广告。根据最终结果，这起诉讼也可能预示着这两大宿敌之间未来的法律角逐。何时以及如何展开尚不确定。目前，我们将看到诺和诺德的诉讼是否会改变礼来销售“瘦身”的方式。

欢迎将您的评论或问题发送给我，电子邮件地址为gaston@k2k.law，或通过Twitter：@gkroub。任何主题建议或想法都非常欢迎。

加斯顿·克鲁布（Gaston Kroub）生活在布鲁克林，是K2K知识产权法律事务所的创始合伙人，该事务所是一家专注于知识产权诉讼的精品律所，同时也是投资界知识产权问题的领先咨询机构。加斯顿的业务重点是知识产权诉讼和相关咨询，特别是专利事务。您可以通过电子邮件gaston@k2k.law与他联系，或在Twitter上关注他：@gkroub。
articles.summary:
For three years straight, I have written on these pages about patent-related issues involving the defining drugs of our lifetimes, GLP-1’s. Let’s go for the fourth year in a row. In 2023, I focused on recently granted patents that the two behemoths in the weight-loss space, Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly, were adding to their growing portfolios protecting their Ozempic/Wegovy and Mounjaro/Zepbound blockbuster franchises. The following year, it was a look at the unsuccessful efforts being pursued by generics hoping to cash in on the insatiable demands for GLP-1 drugs. (Since then, generic Ozempic has become available, but you need a ticket on Air Canada or Air India if you want to pick it up.) And last year, I covered the lawsuit filed by Lilly against a large compounding pharmacy, a major escalation in the multifront (courts and FDA) war fought by the GLP-1 makers against the compounders whose lower-priced offerings were siphoning off about 10% of prescriptions. 

Now, with the threats from compounders and generics mostly contained, we can take a look at the latest piece of GLP-1 news — the surprising false advertising complaint filed by one of the big brands against the other. Before we do so, it is interesting to note that the share price of Lilly since my 2023 column has nearly tripled to its current levels, while that of Novo has taken a significant fall. But even Novo’s GLP-1 revenues have doubled since then, illustrating the continued importance of these drugs to both companies. 

As successful as Novo’s Ozempic/Wegovy franchise has been, Lilly’s dominance in terms of share price appreciation is mirrored by the revenue growth of its Mounjaro/Zepbound products. The latter’s revenue is expected to reach around $45 billion for 2026, a near nine-fold increase since 2023. While Lilly has seized a meatier share of the market than Novo, Novo believes that at least some of Lilly’s success is due to false advertising aimed at misleading customers into believing the relative efficacy of Lilly’s products far exceed those of Novo’s.  According to Novo, when properly compared, the differences in weight-loss potential between the competing drugs are quite close. In Novo’s view, if told the truth, most patients would choose the drug that was less likely to cause them side effects or was priced better, rather than insisting on Lilly’s products because of a mistaken belief that they would lead to more weight loss. Considering the long-term commitment GLP-1 patients often make to their drug of choice, correcting the record is something Novo believes is very important as it tries to capture as much market share as possible before the next generation of GLP-1’s get released. To that end, Novo filed a false advertising lawsuit last week in the District of New Jersey, a filing that was followed a few days later with a motion for preliminary injunction. 

The media reaction to Novo’s filing was immediate, which Novo surely anticipated and almost assuredly welcomed. (Yours truly was even asked to share his views on Novo’s filing with a leading Danish business publication.) Novo’s filing could be viewed as a form of effective counter-advertising, with Novo sending the message that Lilly has to resort to false claims to try to manufacture a competitive advantage against Ozempic/Wegovy. To a consumer, the idea that Lilly’s ads were “untrue enough to get sued” is an easy message to digest and helps generate an effective bit of advertising for Novo, based only on the media attention around the filing. Add in that Novo had sent Lilly a cease-and-desist letter asking for certain changes to Lilly’s advertising before filing, and it would be understandable for a customer to sympathize with the idea that Novo only initiated legal action as a last resort due to Lilly’s intransigence. At the same time, Lilly did at least partially agree to make some changes to its advertising, perhaps setting up a later argument that Novo was overreaching in its claims and that Lilly was the commercially and legally responsible party in the dispute.

With any legal action, however, it is important for the plaintiff to back up the media attention with some success on the merits, particularly when a preliminary injunction is involved. Here, Novo is arguing that Lilly is relying on outdated clinical study results and deliberate dosage miscomparisons to create a narrative that its products are superior. For Novo, the harm is compounded by the scale and reach of Lilly’s marketing, both in terms of social media and television advertisements. Accordingly, Novo’s legal team from Debevoise and Plimpton asks the court to enjoin Lilly from running its current ads. It even goes further, suggesting that the court order Lilly to engage in corrective advertising. For its part, Lilly promises to fight back hard as the case proceeds.

Ultimately, I think this filing is a recognition by Novo that the GLP-1 market in the U.S. is at the stage where these two giants are fighting for every prescription. With the threat from compounded GLP-1’s and generics having arguably been reduced to a manageable level, Novo’s complaint and PI request is a recognition by Novo that it has to get aggressive about acquiring and maintaining market share against Lilly — and that each patient sign-up now, before the launch of more futuristic GLP-1’s, is critical. Thankfully, irrespective of the legal outcome, patients have choices when it comes to their weight-loss and diabetes-management needs. The duopoly at the top of the market is not at risk with this case. What is at stake, however, is how these companies advertise in their bids for more and more market share. Depending on the outcome, this lawsuit may also presage future legal jockeying between these arch competitors. When and how things will unfold is uncertain. For now, we will see if Novo’s lawsuit results in changing how Lilly sells the skinny.

Please feel free to send comments or questions to me at gaston@k2k.law or via Twitter: @gkroub. Any topic suggestions or thoughts are most welcome.

Gaston Kroub lives in Brooklyn and is a founding partner of K2K IP Law, an intellectual property litigation boutique that also serves as a leading consultancy on patent issues for the investment community. Gaston’s practice focuses on intellectual property litigation and related counseling, with a strong focus on patent matters. You can reach him at gaston@k2k.law or follow him on Twitter: @gkroub.

articles.title: Neil Gorsuch Says He Trusts Sonia Sotomayor’s Motives, Even If He Rejects Her Legal Views
articles.content:
编辑注：欢迎来到我们的每日栏目“今日名言”。

我知道她热爱这个国家。她也知道我热爱这个国家。我们都明白，我们是出于内心正确的动机来做这些事的。
——大法官尼尔·戈萨奇在里根公民礼仪与民主论坛上发表讲话时表示，他相信大法官索尼亚·索托马约尔的“良好意愿”，尽管两人在法律问题上存在根本分歧。戈萨奇还指出，他认为美国的民主制度是“脆弱的”，需要通过礼仪来保护它。他说：“我们都在一起。如果我们不团结一致，它就会崩溃。”

斯塔西·扎雷茨基是《法律之上》的执行编辑，自2011年起她一直在此工作。她很乐意听到你的反馈，请随时通过电子邮件与她联系，提供任何线索、问题、评论或批评。你可以在Bluesky、X/Twitter和Threads上关注她，也可以在LinkedIn上与她联系。

本文首发于《法律之上》。
articles.summary:
Ed. note: Welcome to our daily feature, Quote of the Day.

I know she loves this country. She knows I love this country. We know we’re coming at it from the right place internally.

— Justice Neil Gorsuch, in comments given during an appearance at the Reagan Civility and Democracy Forum, where he explained to the audience that he Justice Sonia Sotomayor’s “good intentions,” even though they fundamentally disagree on the law. Gorsuch went on to note that he believed that our democracy is “fragile,” and that civility is needed to keep it safe. “We are all in it together,” he said. “And if we don’t stay all in it together, it will crumble.”

articles.title: Trump Fails To File Promised Birthright Citizenship Rehearing Before Deadline
articles.content:
你们坐好了吗？因为有可能——仅仅是可能——特朗普在撒谎。我知道，我知道。但让我慢慢说。

在挑战宪法第十四修正案公民权保障条款的案件中以5-4或6-3（甚至可能是7-2）判决失利后，特朗普高调要求最高法院给他一个重审机会。政府能否在被同一批法官击败后要求重审成功？极不可能，因为法院上一次在开庭案件中批准重审是在1965年，而上一次重审并推翻原判是在1956年。而1956年的那起案件也创造了历史上唯一成功的先例。

尽管如此，特朗普还是确保所有人在社交媒体上知道，他在案件中发现了新的进展：得克萨斯州一家医院利用最高法院的判决，向试图在美国境内生育的移民推销分娩服务。唯一的问题是，这家医院并没有那么做，而他相信的事情发生在2021年。

唉，考虑到本届政府在法律论据上愿意铤而走险的作风，我们都预料到重审请求会迅速到来。

就像那波涌入境内的刑事犯罪移民潮一样……那其实从未真正发生过。

[悲伤长号声]

我的个人阴谋论是，这次重审马戏团因为托德·布朗奇在司法委员会的连续失败而受到牵连。政府相信——尽管所有迹象都不支持——布朗奇会像去年担任副总检察长时那样轻松通过确认审议，司法部长职位也能在重审截止日期前搞定。

然而，他的投票结果仍在拖延中，而比政府智囊团更有常识的人认为，他们最后需要的就是让布朗奇在镜头前解释，五年前的医院广告如何构成对一个被否定了一个多世纪的法律理论的诚信重审。

要么就是检察长办公室算错了日期，这同样有可能发生。

早前报道：特朗普称最高法院“完全失控”后要求公民权重审

articles.summary:
Are you guys sitting down? Because it’s possible — possible — that Donald Trump might be full of shit. I know, I know. But hear me out.

After losing his challenge to the Fourteenth Amendment’s guarantee of birthright citizenship on a 5-4 or 6-3 (or maybe 7-2?) decision, Donald Trump loudly and proudly demanded the Supreme Court give him a do-over. Would the administration find success seeking a rehearing from the same justices that just swatted it down? Highly unlikely since the Court last granted rehearing in an argued case in 1965, and the last time it reheard a case and actually reversed its decision was in 1956. And that 1956 case still marks the only time in history such an effort has succeeded.

Trump nonetheless made sure everyone on social media knew that he’d found a new development in the case, in the form of a hospital in Texas that used the Supreme Court’s decision as a basis to advertise baby deliveries to migrants seeking to give birth on American soil. The only problem was the hospital did NOT do that and what he thinks it did happened in 2021.

Alas, given this administration’s willingness to run head first into the studs with its legal arguments, we all expected the rehearing request would arrive forthwith.

But just like the mass wave of criminal immigrants surging across the border… it was never actually real.

[Sad trombone.]

My personal conspiracy theory here is that this rehearing circus sideshow fell victim to Todd Blanche’s repeated failures before the Senate Judiciary Committee. The administration believed — despite all indications to the contrary — that Blanche would cruise through confirmation just like he did last year for the Deputy AG job and the Attorney General position could be all sewn up in time for the rehearing deadline.

Instead, his vote is still getting carried over and someone with more sense than traditionally displayed by the Trump Peanut Gallery decided the last thing they needed was to put Blanche on camera trying to explain how a hospital ad from five years ago made for a good faith rehearing on a legal theory that’s been roundly rejected for over a century.

Either that or the Solicitor General’s office just miscounted days, which is honestly just as likely.
